title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money and Dust—What Our Mutual Friend Promises

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, devoted, sometimes argumentative reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel.
Our Mutual Friend was published in 1864 and 1865, and it may be the strangest, richest, most unsettling thing Dickens ever wrote.
It begins with a body pulled from the Thames, and it ends — well, we won't get ahead of ourselves.
Today we're starting at the beginning: the novel's great founding image — dust.
Dust as money, dust as waste, dust as what society sweeps under the carpet and what it's ultimately built on.
I'm joined by three people whose company I find genuinely indispensable for a novel this large and this demanding.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — with joy in every gear.
She will tell us how Dickens builds his effects — sentence by sentence, image by image.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class and power.
He will keep us honest about who the dust actually belongs to, and who gets buried in it.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has been re-reading this novel since her teens — which gives her something no one else at this table has: a lifelong ear for it.
She'll be reading passages aloud, and I suspect she'll make us hear things we've walked past a dozen times.
So — let's begin with the dust.
Daniel, Dickens wastes no time introducing us to the Dust Contractor — this grotesque, growling old man who has turned rubbish into a fortune.
What does that image — a man who literally lives inside a mountain of dust — announce to you about what this novel is going to be?
It announces, immediately and without apology, that this is a novel about accumulation — about where wealth actually comes from.
The Dust Contractor doesn't inherit a fortune or earn it through gentlemanly trade.
He takes what society discards — everything it throws away — and he piles it into a mountain and calls it capital.
And Dickens describes this estate with a kind of savage geological poetry that I think is astonishing.
"Coal-dust, vegetable-dust, bone-dust, crockery dust, rough dust and sifted dust,—all manner of Dust."
That list — that relentless catalogue — is Dickens showing you the entire material basis of this society reduced to refuse.
Coal, vegetables, bone — the labour and sustenance of people — and it all ends up here, on this man's estate, earning him a mountain.
That's not comedy. That's diagnosis.
And notice the craft in that list — it's not random.
Dickens moves from specific named dusts — coal, vegetable, bone, crockery — to the abstract categories: rough and sifted.
He's drilling down into particularity and then pulling back out to the universal — and the final word, capitalised, "Dust," acts like a gavel.
It closes the case. This is what everything is.
There's also the volcano comparison — the old man "threw up his own mountain range, like an old volcano" — and that geological metaphor does something crucial.
It makes his greed feel primordial — not a personal failing but a force of nature, ancient and destructive.
Dickens is already telling us this isn't a story about one greedy man.
What strikes me is the narrator's tone in all of this — because it's being relayed at a dinner party.
Mortimer is telling the story of this fortune as an after-dinner entertainment, and the guests find it amusing.
And Dickens is watching them find it amusing — and finding that fact rather damning.
The comedy is real — I laugh every time at "all manner of Dust" — but the laughter catches in your throat if you're paying attention.
This is Dickens doing what he does better than almost anyone — letting you enjoy the joke and then making you complicit in it.
That complicity is exactly what he returns to later — and much more directly.

There's a passage later in the novel where the narrator turns and addresses the governing classes by name — "my lords and gentlemen and honourable boards" — and the satire has completely shed its comedy.
He's describing the dust heap again — the mountain of social failure — and the warning he issues is explicit and chilling.
"You must off with your honourable coats for the removal of it, and fall to the work with the power of all the queen's horses and all the queen's men, or it will come rushing down and bury us alive."
He's saying: the mountain you've built from neglect is not stable.
It will collapse. And when it does, it will take everyone with it.
That's not a polite Victorian reformist plea. That's a structural prediction.
And the nursery-rhyme echo — "all the queen's horses and all the queen's men" — is doing real work there.
It's Humpty Dumpty. The state, for all its pomp, cannot put this back together.
The allusion makes the warning feel almost folkloric — inevitable, ancient — which amplifies the dread rather than softening it.
And the fog passage sets all of this in physical space — because it's not just dust that fills London, it's fog.
I keep coming back to that description of the city choking on itself.
Dickens writes that the fog moves from grey at the edges to dark yellow, then brown, then browner, then rusty-black at the heart of the City.

"Animate London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing, and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither."
That division — visible and invisible, wholly neither — feels to me like the novel's whole predicament.
The poor are there. The suffering is there. But the fog makes it possible not to see.
That image — London as a city that has perfected the art of not seeing — feels like the right note to carry us into our first proper section.
We'll be looking at characters — the people who move through this fog, who live on or near the dust heap — and what Dickens makes of them.

segments.title: The Architecture of Disguise: How Dickens Buries John Harmon

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — sentence by sentence, idea by idea.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the most elaborate narrative sleights of hand in all of Victorian fiction.
John Harmon — presumed drowned, wanted by the police, mourned by no one who knows the truth — is walking the streets of London in plain sight.
He is John Rokesmith. He is Julius Handford. He is, somehow, all three at once.
With me today are three readers who know exactly how Dickens pulls this off — and why it matters so much more than a clever plot trick.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens for the architecture — the structural choices that make a scene do ten things at once.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who sees the Harmon disguise not as a romantic device but as a ruthless exposure of how money and class shape every identity in this novel.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who cares above all about the experience of reading — what it feels like when Dickens lets you in on the secret.
Eleanor, let's start with the moment Dickens shows his hand — or rather, shows us a face beneath the face.
What strikes me first about that passage is how Dickens handles the grammar of transformation.
He doesn't say Harmon takes off a disguise. He says he ceases to be one man and becomes another.
There's a passive quality to it — as if the identity shifts around him rather than being shed like a coat.
And then comes this extraordinary formulation. Dickens writes it twice in the same paragraph.
"became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world."
He then applies the exact same phrase to Rokesmith — as if to say these three identities are equally real, equally present, and none is the original.
The repetition is the argument. Dickens is saying: identity is not a stable core you return to. It is a surface you inhabit.
Eleanor is right that it's not a simple unmasking. But I want to press on what that repeated phrase actually contains.
"Lost" and "wanted" — those are police words. Those are words from a missing-persons notice on a London wall.
Harmon's real name is already the property of the state — defined by what the law is searching for.
And why is he in this position at all? Because his father's fortune has turned him into a commodity before he could speak for himself.
Dickens makes this explicit in the analysis of his first deception. He writes of
"the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence."
The disguise doesn't come from cunning. It comes from a psyche deformed by inherited money and a loveless childhood.
That is the novel's claim: the system that produces great fortunes also produces people who cannot trust themselves to exist without a mask.
What I keep returning to, as a reader, is how Dickens uses the word "ghost."
When Rokesmith wakes after his night of — and this is the novel's own phrase — piling earth above John Harmon, the language becomes genuinely eerie.
"No ghost should trouble Mr and Mrs Boffin's peace; invisible and voiceless, the ghost should look on for a little while longer at the state of existence out of which it had departed."
He refers to himself in the third person. As a ghost. Already.
That's not just a plot mechanism. That is a man who has genuinely stepped outside his own life and is watching it from somewhere cold.
And the tenderness toward the Boffins — "no ghost should trouble their peace" — makes it unbearably poignant. He is protecting them from himself.
Caroline's point about the third person is structurally crucial, because Dickens is doing the same thing at the narrative level.
He actually steps into the text himself to explain his design — which is almost unheard of for him at this point in his career.
He writes, in the postscript that functions almost as a manifesto:

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
He's not apologising for the ambiguity. He's taking credit for it.
The concealment and the revelation were always the same gesture — aimed at different readers, timed differently, but both intentional.
And yet there is something I find morally uncomfortable in the scheme itself — separate from Dickens's narrative craft.
Consider the plot as Harmon himself describes it in that remarkable confession.
"The plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way."
A man of wealth and legal claim over a woman disguises himself as a working-class sailor to surveil her without her knowledge.
The novel asks us to find this romantic. But it is also a portrait of power — of someone who has the luxury of choosing his own identity while Bella has no such freedom.
He tests her. She cannot test him. The asymmetry is the point — and Dickens, to his credit, does not entirely let Harmon off the hook for it.
I take Daniel's point entirely, and it's one I wrestle with every time I re-read this section.
But what makes me hold on to Harmon's side of it is the passage where he explains the decision to stay dead.
He writes that while lying in that public-house bed, recovering,
"the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella."
"Proving" is such a strange, legal, almost inhuman word to use of the woman you intend to marry.
And yet the dread that drives it is real — he is terrified of perpetuating his father's curse, the way money has poisoned every relationship he has ever witnessed.
He is not a cold man performing an experiment. He is a frightened man grasping for the one form of honesty still available to him.
And Dickens knew — with extraordinary lucidity — how difficult it was to sustain all of this across nineteen months of serial publication.
He describes it in the postscript with something close to pride and exhaustion in equal measure.

"To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out, another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and the most difficult part of my design."
"Always working itself out" — that's the phrase I can't get past. It's organic. The secret has its own momentum.
He also uses the image of the story-weaver at his loom — able to see the whole pattern, while readers encounter only one thread at a time.
That image goes to the heart of what this entire disguise plot is doing: Harmon sees the full design of his own life; everyone else sees only a fragment.
Eleanor, Daniel, Caroline — what you've laid out is the extraordinary double structure of this disguise: it's a plot mechanism and a psychological portrait simultaneously.
A man who has been taught by everything in his life that wealth corrupts identity, choosing to be dead so that his own identity might, for once, be clean.
In our next segment, we'll follow the consequences of that choice — and ask whether the novel truly lets him escape the father's curse, or only defers it.

segments.title: Reading Bella Aloud: The Music of a Woman Learning to Want Less

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're doing something we've been saving for a while: reading Bella Wilfer aloud, closely, slowly.
Bella is one of Dickens's most intricate constructions — a woman whose moral journey is inseparable from the way she speaks to herself.
Caroline Woodcourt is our guide for this segment — she's been re-reading these passages with the ear of someone who genuinely loves the verbal texture of the novel.
Caroline, where do you want to begin?
I want to begin with Bella alone in her room, at the looking-glass.
Because this is where Dickens does something I find almost miraculous — he stages a character's self-knowledge as a comic scene.
She's just come away from Mr Boffin, who has said something entirely sensible about money and ambition.
And she agrees with him — completely — and yet she finds herself despising him for saying it.
Listen to how she puts it to herself:

'What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it.'
The rhythm of that is extraordinary — the repeated 'I am sure' that isn't sure at all.
And then she turns on herself with this wonderful phrase:
'Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
She prosecutes herself in the mirror, and the jury is also Bella.
'You inconsistent little Beast' — there's a whole moral education in that phrase, delivered entirely by the defendant.
Eleanor, you've written about how Dickens distributes interiority across his characters — does this scene strike you the same way?
Enormously — and I'd add something structural to what Caroline's hearing in the rhythm.
Dickens gives Bella free indirect thought — he slides inside her consciousness — but the looking-glass makes it theatrical.
She's not just thinking; she's performing her self-accusation to a visible audience: herself.
That's a very precise narrative choice — it externalises what would otherwise be silent guilt, and it lets the comedy do moral work.
The name she calls herself — Beast — is both self-lacerating and oddly affectionate, which is exactly Bella's problem.
Yes — and what's so tender about it is that she can see herself clearly, she just can't yet change.
Which brings me to the scene with Lizzie Hexam, which I think is the pivot of Bella's whole arc.
Before Lizzie, Bella is what the narrator calls, precisely:
'wayward, playful, affectionate nature, giddy for want of the weight of some sustaining purpose, and capricious because it was always fluttering among little things'
'Giddy for want of the weight' — I have to stop there.
That is one of the finest descriptions of a kind of moral vacancy in all of Dickens.
She doesn't lack intelligence — she lacks ballast.
'Fluttering among little things' — the image is physical, almost entomological.
Dickens makes her lightness visible as a structural condition, not a character flaw — she needs weight, a purpose to orbit.
And then Lizzie gives her the first glimpse of what an unselfish love actually looks like.
The narrator's line about that moment is devastatingly simple:
'Bella sat enchained by the deep, unselfish passion of this girl or woman of her own age, courageously revealing itself in the confidence of her sympathetic perception of its truth.'
'And yet she had never experienced anything like it, or thought of the existence of anything like it.'
That second sentence is where it lands — 'the existence of anything like it.'
Not merely that she hadn't felt it — she hadn't conceived it was possible.
Daniel, I want to bring you in here — because Caroline and Eleanor are describing Bella's interiority with a lot of sympathy.
Do you read the same passages differently?
Not differently so much as — additionally.
The comic self-accusation Caroline describes is brilliant, but I want to notice what Bella is accusing herself of.
She calls herself a 'mercenary wretch' — and she's right about that.
But the novel is careful to show where that mercenariness came from — it wasn't innate, it was cultivated.
The passage with Lizzie is the turning point — Lizzie's selfless love makes Bella recognise something.
Listen to what she actually does:
'There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?'
And then she gives herself, and I love this detail, 'a penitential poke in the side.'
The body registers the moral failure that the conscious mind is still half-evading.
'A penitential poke in the side' — I've always loved that phrase enormously.
It's absurd, but it's also precisely what remorse feels like before it becomes action.
And by the time we reach her conversation with her father, something has solidified.
She says it simply, directly, and it is the most important sentence she speaks:
'You don't know, Pa, what a shocking creature I was growing, when he saved me from myself!'
'He saved me from myself' — that's not the language of romance.
That's the language of someone who recognises she was in genuine danger.
And look at the journey from 'inconsistent little Beast' to 'shocking creature I was growing.'
The first is playful self-accusation. The second is reckoning.
Dickens has moved her across three registers — the comic, the tender, the moral — and he's done it entirely through how she addresses herself.
No other character in the novel gets that kind of architecturally sustained interior development.
From the looking-glass to the reckoning — that's a beautifully compressed way to hear the whole arc.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the world Bella was being shaped by — the Golden Dustman and the corruption at the heart of the Boffin household.

segments.title: Who Profits? The Dust Heaps as System

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully — to see what's inside.
Today's segment goes to the heart of the book's economic imagination: the Dust Heaps.
Mountains of Victorian refuse — ash, cinders, bones, rags — that turn out to be worth a fortune.
Dickens uses them to ask a question that still cuts: who profits from the waste a society produces, and what does that wealth do to the people who inherit it?
With me to work through this are three wonderful readers of the novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and thinks obsessively about how novelists construct their effects — the architecture beneath the surface.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and he has a lot to say about this particular segment of Our Mutual Friend.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel for decades and brings the most important perspective of all: what it actually feels like to read it.
Let's start with Mr Boffin himself — the Golden Dustman — and what Dickens reveals in the way he talks about his inheritance.
What strikes me first is the precision Dickens gives Boffin when he talks about the Mounds.
This is a man who has been written off as uneducated, as simple — and Dickens immediately complicates that.
Boffin says, and I want to read this exactly as it sits on the page:
'I ain't a scholar in much, Rokesmith, but I'm a pretty fair scholar in dust. I can price the Mounds to a fraction.'
A scholar in dust — that phrase is doing enormous work.
Dickens is constructing a kind of counter-expertise: the knowledge that polite society ignores, that comes from handling what polite society throws away.
It's a radical little move, buried in the comedy.
Eleanor's right that it's radical, and I'd push that even further.
The Mounds are not accidental wealth — they are the accumulated surplus of an entire urban economy.
Every shovelful represents labour — often the labour of the very poor — that has been sorted, classified, monetised.
And the moment the Boffins inherit that fortune, watch what happens to them socially.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary image when the Boffins move into their mansion:
'behold all manner of crawling, creeping, fluttering, and buzzing creatures, attracted by the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!'
The wealth hasn't changed its nature — it's still dust — but it has acquired a different name: gold.
And the insects swarm accordingly.
That list of creatures — crawling, creeping, fluttering, buzzing — you feel it in your skin when you read it aloud.
Dickens is not being subtle here and he doesn't want to be.
But what moves me is the detail about the mansion itself — Boffin regards it, Dickens says,
'like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites.'
An aristocratic family cheese.
It's so absurd and so precise — a thing that breeds decay from within, that has ripened past any useful purpose.
And Boffin accepts the parasites as a kind of tax — a Legacy Duty, Dickens calls it — which is a very dark joke indeed.
The cheese image works because Dickens collapses the distance between aristocratic aspiration and rot.
The Mounds were literally decomposing matter that generated wealth — and now the mansion is doing the same thing socially.
It's a structural rhyme across the whole novel — waste producing value, value producing new forms of waste.
And the charity letters that flood the Secretary's desk are exactly that — a new form of waste dressed in the language of benevolence.
The charity letters passage is one of the great satirical set pieces in the novel — let me read part of it because the detail is extraordinary.
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
The narration has become the envelope — Dickens mimes the physical object before we even read the letter inside.
And the Duke's postscript — 'The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas' — is of course the whole point.
The aristocracy has simply found a more elegant mechanism for extracting money from newly wealthy people desperate for social legitimacy.
The dust heap and the ducal letter are the same transaction — dirt moving upward through the class system.
And what Dickens does brilliantly is show that none of this wealth reaches the people who need it.
There's a passage later in the novel where the narrator speaks with barely contained fury about exactly that failure.

'when we have got things to the pass that with an enormous treasure at disposal to relieve the poor, the best of the poor detest our mercies, hide their heads from us, and shame us by starving to death in the midst of us'—
'it is a pass impossible of prosperity, impossible of continuance.'
That repetition — impossible of prosperity, impossible of continuance — has the weight of a verdict.
He's not writing social comedy any more. He's writing something closer to prophecy.
And note how Dickens frames those lords and gentlemen and honourable boards — he's addressing them directly, in the second person.
The novel has shed its fictional skin for a moment and become an indictment.
It's a structural gamble — stepping outside the story — and it works because everything before it has earned that fury.
The Mounds, the mansion, the Duke's letter, the crawling creatures — all of it builds to that sentence.
What Dickens understood — perhaps more clearly than he knew how to say theoretically — is that the system isn't failing.
It's succeeding at something different from what it claims to be doing.
The charities recirculate money among the respectable classes. The Mounds enrich a single family. The poor starve in the midst of it.
That is not malfunction. That is the design.
That phrase — the design — is going to stay with us, I think, as we move through the rest of the novel.
We've seen the Dust Heaps as inheritance, as social magnet, as failed philanthropy, and as a system that produces its own critique.
In our next segment, we'll follow the money further — into the lives of the characters it corrupts, tempts, and occasionally redeems.

segments.title: Bella's Reckoning: Craft and Consequence in a Novel About Gold

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's great sprawling novel of money, identity, and transformation apart — slowly, carefully, and with real pleasure.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the novel's most brilliantly engineered storylines: Bella Wilfer's moral reckoning with wealth.
To take it apart with me are three readers whose perspectives couldn't be more different — or more complementary.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who's fascinated by the architecture of how Dickens builds his effects — sentence by sentence, image by image.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomies of class power — and he'll push us to ask who really benefits from Bella's transformation.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who brings us back to what it actually feels like on the page.
Eleanor, let's start with you — because Dickens opens the question of whether Bella is deceived or whether Mr Boffin is genuinely corrupted with a sentence that feels almost like a trumpet blast.
That sentence is one of the great Dickensian rhetorical pivots — and I think it's worth hearing it exactly as he wrote it.
He poses it as a genuine either/or:
'Dross' is doing enormous work there — it's the residue left after metal is smelted, the worthless material you're left with when the gold is gone.
Dickens has inverted the alchemical metaphor: normally the furnace of proof purifies you and you come out gold.
Here, the furnace is wealth itself — and the question is whether it burns away everything that was decent in the man.
What I love structurally is the sentence that follows: 'Ill news travels fast. We shall know full soon.'
That 'we' is the narrator pulling us into the confidence of the plot — Dickens knew all along.
Eleanor is right that the metallurgical metaphor is precise — but I want to press on what it means that wealth is the furnace.
Dickens is not writing a parable about one man's weakness.
He is making a structural claim: that the institution of money corrupts anyone it touches, regardless of their native goodness.
The Golden Dustman is a brilliant figure precisely because his wealth comes from dust — from the refuse of society, the accumulated waste of other people's lives.
So when money makes him mean, Dickens is telling us something about where that money came from in the first place.
What strikes me — reading it again — is how much Dickens trusts the reader to feel the horror alongside Bella.
She is watching someone she admired turn into something she barely recognises — and Dickens captures that in Mr Boffin's face.
There's that later passage where Bella sees him restored — and the question Dickens frames is almost unbearable in its simplicity.
That phrase — 'crooked lines' — does what only Dickens can do: it makes a moral condition visible on a body.
The face was a ledger. And now the debts have been cleared.
Caroline's point about the face as ledger goes right to the heart of what Dickens is doing with Bella's arc, structurally.
Bella must be tested — that's not just an emotional requirement, it's a formal one.
And Dickens has Bella herself demand that test — which is a remarkable piece of characterisation.
She says to John — and this is Bella at her finest:
She is not asking for reassurance — she is asking to be proven.
That is the difference between a sentimental heroine and a Dickensian one.
I want to read that demand for a trial slightly differently from Eleanor — though I think Eleanor's reading is the one Dickens intends.
The question I keep returning to is: what exactly has Bella been saved from, and what has she been saved for?
R. Wilfer tells us — in his gently comic, roundabout way — that Bella saw prosperity spoiling Mr Boffin and refused to follow.
And the passage is worth hearing in full because the syntax enacts the moral argument:
Notice what Dickens does with that list — right and wrong, true and false, just and unjust — paired opposites marching forward like a litany.
Bella is being offered a price. She refuses it. That is the novel's moral spine.
Daniel's reading of that list moved me — because it gets at something Dickens does that I find almost overwhelming when I re-read it.
Bella, at the end, doesn't claim she has become worthy — she confesses her unworthiness with complete conviction.
She says — covering her face with her hands, which is a beautiful stage direction:
That last phrase — 'so unworthy a wife' — after all that extravagant generosity from the Boffins — is genuinely affecting.
She's not performing humility. She means it. And that difference is what the whole arc has been built to demonstrate.
What I hear in all three of your readings is a novel that refuses easy virtue — where being good is something you have to choose, under pressure, and keep choosing.
Bella earns her happiness not by being naturally good, but by recognising what money costs — and deciding it's too high a price.
In our next segment, we'll follow the gold in the other direction — away from the Boffins and down into the river, where the novel's other great reckoning is waiting.

segments.title: The Laugh That Catches You: Dickens's Comic Humanity in the Margins

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — slowly, lovingly, and with great attention to what makes it tick.
I'm your host, and today's segment asks a question that sounds simple but opens into something rich: what does Dickens do when he's being funny?
Not funny in a broad, theatrical way — but funny in the margins, in the throwaway lines, in the characters who exist at the edges of the plot and yet somehow stay with you longest.
To help us explore that, I'm delighted to have three extraordinary readers with me.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads with a craftsperson's eye — she sees how the machinery works, and makes you love it all the more for understanding it.
Daniel Rosen reads novels as social documents — he wants to know who holds power, who is crushed by it, and how laughter itself can be a political act.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived inside this novel for decades — she reads it as a reader first, and she's never lost that original thrill.
Caroline, let's begin with you — because you've brought us one of the novel's great comic set pieces, Eugene Wrayburn conducting Mortimer on a tour of his chambers.
What's Dickens actually doing there?
The first time I read that passage I laughed out loud, and then immediately read it again more slowly — which is the surest sign Dickens is doing something unusual.
Eugene has set up this immaculate little kitchen — miniature flour-barrel, rolling-pin, spice-box, roasting jack — and he catalogs it with enormous solemnity.
And then he delivers this line with the gravity of a man announcing a philosophical discovery.
'The moral influence of these objects, in forming the domestic virtues, may have an immense influence upon me.'
The joke is the sincerity — or rather the performance of sincerity by a man who couldn't be less sincere.
Eugene has no intention of using any of this equipment — the pigeon-holes, the secretaire, the charming kettle — for anything resembling their stated purpose.
And yet Dickens lets him deliver the whole speech with the air of — and this is Dickens's own phrase — 'a philosopher lecturing a disciple.'
That's the thing about Eugene: his idleness has the completeness of a vocation.
What strikes me structurally is that Eugene builds the joke in layers — and Dickens times each layer with enormous precision.
First we get the inventory — 'miniature flour-barrel, rolling-pin, spice-box, shelf of brown jars' — which is funny in its sheer specificity.
Then the moral lecture, which escalates the absurdity.
But the real coup is the pigeonhole system — where Eugene demonstrates his method for managing bills by filing them away and then treating the act of filing as equivalent to paying.
He says — and this is the sentence I can never quite get over —
'I docket it neatly at the secretaire, Jones, and I put it into pigeonhole J. It's the next thing to a receipt and is quite as satisfactory to me.'
The logic is absolutely watertight within the terms Eugene has constructed.
Dickens is showing us how ideology works — how a class that doesn't need to pay its bills constructs a perfectly coherent philosophy in which not paying them is a form of virtue.
Eleanor's put her finger on exactly the right nerve.
Eugene is performing the forms of bourgeois domestic virtue — the kitchen, the system, the method — while being completely insulated from any need to actually live by them.
That charming kitchen is never going to be used for cooking.
But its existence allows Eugene to perform virtue — to himself, to Mortimer, and in some sense to the class he represents.
And Dickens makes it funny rather than simply damning — which is the shrewder move, because satire that makes you laugh gets past your defenses in a way that direct indictment never does.
That contrast — form without function, method without purpose — turns up everywhere in this novel.
Mr Podsnap is the most extreme version of it.
Where Eugene performs domesticity, Podsnap performs moral judgment — and uses it to make the uncomfortable world simply disappear.
The passage I've been thinking about has Podsnap confronted with something inconvenient — people who've lived beyond their means and gone to smash.
And his response is one of the most perfectly constructed dismissals in English fiction.
'It is an odious subject, an offensive subject, a subject that makes me sick, and I—'
And then Dickens completes the sentence for him with that arm gesture — 'his favourite right-arm flourish which sweeps away everything and settles it for ever.'
The dash after 'I—' is doing so much work.
Podsnap doesn't finish the sentence because he doesn't need to — the arm completes it.
That dash is extraordinary craft.
Dickens is using punctuation as stage direction — the unfinished sentence enacts the very thing it describes.
Podsnap's rhetoric sweeps things away, so the sentence itself sweeps away — it refuses to arrive at its own conclusion.

And then the narrator steps in and sweeps these 'inconveniently unexplainable wretches' off the face of the universe — ventriloquizing Podsnap while making absolutely clear how monstrous the gesture is.
Free indirect discourse used as moral indictment — it's one of Dickens's sharpest tools in this novel.
And what Podsnap is sweeping away is poverty — actual human beings destroyed by a system that Podsnap himself benefits from and refuses to examine.
The comedy is the horror.
We laugh at Podsnap's gesture — it is funny, the arm is perfectly rendered — but Dickens won't let the laugh be comfortable.
The phrase 'off the face of the universe' is just slightly too grand, too total — it tips the satire into something darker than mere ridicule.
Let's move from the drawing room to somewhere altogether more unexpected — a police inspector and a dead body.
Caroline, you've also brought us the Night Inspector's remarkable meditation on murder — which is one of the strangest comic passages in the entire novel.
Strange is exactly the word.
The Inspector is thinking about whether the mysterious Handford might have committed a murder — and he reflects on murder in the most matter-of-fact professional terms.
The line that gets me every time is this one.
'Burglary or pocket-picking wanted 'prenticeship. Not so, murder. We were all of us up to that.'
'We were all of us up to that' — delivered with the same professional equanimity you might use to discuss filing paperwork.
It's funny, but it's also deeply unsettling — because of course he's right.
Murder requires no training.
And then he reflects that bodies don't give you signs — 'you never got a sign out of bodies if it was ever so' — with a mild regret, as if discussing an unreliable witness.
What Dickens is doing technically with the Inspector is stripping away almost all the narrative infrastructure — there's barely any verbiage linking the reported thoughts.
It reads like abbreviated notes — 'Might have been Stomach and not Mind. If so, rum stomach. But to be sure there were rum everythings.'
The repetition of 'rum' there is doing something very precise — it's the Inspector's word for anything that defies tidy categorization.
And by the third use, 'there were rum everythings,' the world itself has become ungovernable — in a single throwaway clause.
The Inspector represents a kind of institutional intelligence — professional, undisturbed, completely at home with death.
And the comedy of 'we were all of us up to that' is that it levels the social hierarchy entirely.
Burglary is a trade — it belongs to the poor, to those who've served their apprenticeship in need.
But murder — murder anyone can manage.
The Inspector doesn't intend that as a democratic statement, but Dickens absolutely does.
One more character who deserves his moment — and this one is perhaps the most purely loveable comic figure in the novel.
Mr Boffin, standing alone in the moonlight, reeling from Silas Wegg's reading of Roman history.
This passage is one of my favourite things in the entire novel — and I say that as someone who finds it very hard to choose.
Boffin has just had Wegg read to him about Commodus and Vitellius, and he's been utterly overwhelmed by the sheer excess of classical history.
Listen to how he processes it.

'Commodious fights in that wild-beast-show, seven hundred and thirty-five times, in one character only! As if that wasn't stunning enough, a hundred lions is turned into the same wild-beast-show all at once!'
'As if that wasn't stunning enough' — twice! — is the rhythm of a man who cannot believe the world keeps escalating against him.
And then 'Vittle-us — and well named too — eats six millions' worth, English money, in seven months.'
That parenthetical — 'and well named too' — is Boffin making sense of history the only way he can, through appetite and nickname.
What Dickens has done with Boffin's syntax is quite brilliant.
The repetition of 'as if that wasn't stunning enough' enacts the accumulation it describes — each clause adds a new impossible fact, and the structural echo makes it feel genuinely vertiginous.
And then Dickens lands the passage with a sentence of pure resigned humanity.
'I didn't think this morning there was half so many Scarers in Print. But I'm in for it now!'
'Scarers' with a capital S — as if they deserve the designation of a proper category of things, like tigers or taxes.
And 'I'm in for it now' is the sound of a man who has decided, against all the evidence, to continue his education.
Boffin is one of the novel's strangest figures, because Dickens genuinely loves him — without condescension, without irony.
Here is a man made rich by dust and rubbish, standing in moonlight, trying to absorb Roman imperial excess — and being staggered by it in exactly the way any honest person would be.
The comedy doesn't diminish him.
And there's something quietly pointed about Boffin — a man of no formal education — being more morally alert than almost anyone in the novel's upper reaches.
Vittellius eating six million pounds' worth and Podsnap sweeping the poor off the face of the universe — they're the same gesture, really.
What a connection — Boffin horrified by ancient excess, and Podsnap performing a very modern version of it.
I think what today's conversation has uncovered is that Dickens's comedy is never decorative — it's doing the novel's hardest moral work, often in the passages we might be tempted to skip past.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt — and to you for listening.
We'll be back soon with another segment of Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

segments.title: Closing: Resurrection and Value—What the Novel Teaches

utterances.text: We've arrived at the end of our journey through Our Mutual Friend, and what a journey it has been.
This final segment asks the largest question the novel poses: what does it ultimately teach us about value, resurrection, and the possibility of change?
Dickens ends this book in multiple registers at once — comic, tender, polemical, elegiac.
I want to start with Eleanor, who has been tracking the novel's architecture all episode.
How does the structure of the ending reflect the structure of everything that came before?
The ending is, formally speaking, a series of restorations — and Dickens is meticulous about the order in which he performs them.
John and Bella Harmon don't just reclaim their name and fortune — they actively go back and repair the damage that John's fictitious death caused.
Listen to how Dickens describes it — this magnificent, almost legalistic sentence.

"Mr and Mrs John Harmon's first delightful occupation was, to set all matters right that had strayed in any way wrong, or that might, could, would, or should, have strayed in any way wrong, while their name was in abeyance."
"Might, could, would, or should" — that cascade of modals is comic, but it's also moral.
Dickens is insisting that responsibility extends even to the merely possible wrongs, not just the actual ones.
That's a radical ethical standard dressed up as comic bureaucratic language.
And yet the novel is honest about who gets to enact that restoration and on what terms.
It's John Harmon — the man with the fortune — who gets to decide which wrongs count and which people are owed protection.
The dolls' dressmaker, Riah, even Inspector — they are received into a circle of patronage, not granted autonomous standing.
And then there's that extraordinary detail about Inspector, which is so darkly funny it almost distracts you from what it reveals.
He "didn't stand to lose a farthing" through Mr Harmon's coming to life, but was quite as well satisfied as if that gentleman had been barbarously murdered, and he had pocketed the government reward.
The state's representative is indifferent to whether a man lives or dies, so long as his own accounting comes out right.
Dickens is not letting the institutions off the hook, even in a comic resolution.
What strikes me, reading these closing chapters again, is how tenderly Dickens handles Bella's transformation.
She was the novel's most mercenary figure at the start — and she knows it.
She can't quite believe she deserves what she's been given.
There's a moment where she asks John a question that I find almost unbearably moving in its honesty.
"Are you sure, John dear; are you absolutely certain in your innermost heart of hearts—?"
She can't even finish the sentence.
The dash does all the work — the guilt she still carries is there in that silence.
And that, to me, is the novel's real test of whether change is genuine: it's not the transformation itself, it's the memory the transformed person keeps of who they were.
Caroline's point about memory connects to something structural that haunts the whole novel.
Dickens opens the book with the river as carrier of death, and he closes it with the river as carrier of forgetting.
There is that extraordinary early passage where the Harmon Murder itself — the crime at the novel's origin — simply dissolves.

"like the tides on which it had been borne to the knowledge of men, the Harmon Murder went up and down, and ebbed and flowed, now in the town, now in the country, now among palaces, now among hovels, now among lords and ladies and gentlefolks, now among labourers and hammerers and ballast-heavers, until at last, after a long interval of slack water it got out to sea and drifted away."
That list — palaces, hovels, lords, labourers — traverses the entire social hierarchy in a single sentence.
The murder doesn't resolve — it diffuses.
Society absorbs the scandal and moves on, which is itself a kind of verdict on that society.
And if we want to understand what Dickens thought that society was actually doing to its most vulnerable people, we can't avoid the postscript on the Poor Law.
This is Dickens stepping out from behind the fiction entirely — speaking in his own voice, with barely contained fury.
He anticipates every objection from the defenders of the law, and demolishes them one by one.
Then he delivers his verdict — and it is worth hearing in full.
"I believe there has been in England, since the days of the Stuarts, no law so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law habitually so ill-supervised."

"In the majority of the shameful cases of disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known language could say no more of their lawlessness."
"Known language could say no more" — that is a man who has reached the limit of what words can do, and saying so is itself an act of witness.
Betty Higden died fleeing an institution that the law itself mandated and tolerated.
That is not sentiment — that is a documented social fact, and Dickens knew it.
What I keep returning to, at the end of this novel, is how much Dickens trusts his readers to hold contradictions.
The comic and the tragic are not separate registers here — they're braided together.
Inspector's cheerful indifference to whether a man lived or died sits in the same book as Bella's trembling question to John.
Both are true accounts of the same world.
And maybe that is what makes this the most complete of all Dickens's novels, to my mind.
It earns its joy honestly, without flinching from what the world actually costs.
That feels like the right place to end — and to begin rereading.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel that earns more with every encounter — more comedy, more darkness, more craft than you remembered.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has done the novel genuine justice.
For listeners who want to go deeper, the novel rewards close reading at every level — from the sentence up to the full tidal sweep.
This has been Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Thank you for listening.

It was a foggy day in London, and the fog was heavy and dark. Animate
      London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing,
      and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose
      between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither.
      Gaslights flared in the shops with a haggard and unblest air, as knowing
      themselves to be night-creatures that had no business abroad under the
      sun; while the sun itself when it was for a few moments dimly indicated
      through circling eddies of fog, showed as if it had gone out and were
      collapsing flat and cold. Even in the surrounding country it was a foggy
      day, but there the fog was grey, whereas in London it was, at about the
      boundary line, dark yellow, and a little within it brown, and then
      browner, and then browner, until at the heart of the City—which call
      Saint Mary Axe—it was rusty-black. From any point of the high ridge
      of land northward, it might have been discerned that the loftiest
      buildings made an occasional struggle to get their heads above the foggy
      sea, and especially that the great dome of Saint Paul’s seemed to die
      hard; but this was not perceivable in the streets at their feet, where the
      whole metropolis was a heap of vapour charged with muffled sound of
      wheels, and enfolding a gigantic catarrh.

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.

When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of

To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out,
      another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a
      pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and
      the most difficult part of my design. Its difficulty was much enhanced by
      the mode of publication; for, it would be very unreasonable to expect that
      many readers, pursuing a story in portions from month to month through
      nineteen months, will, until they have it before them complete, perceive
      the relations of its finer threads to the whole pattern which is always
      before the eyes of the story-weaver at his loom. Yet, that I hold the
      advantages of the mode of publication to outweigh its disadvantages, may
      be easily believed of one who revived it in the Pickwick Papers after long
      disuse, and has pursued it ever since.

And now, in the blooming summer days, behold Mr and Mrs Boffin established
      in the eminently aristocratic family mansion, and behold all manner of
      crawling, creeping, fluttering, and buzzing creatures, attracted by the
      gold dust of the Golden Dustman!
c17:p0.summary: The Boffins are now established in their grand mansion and immediately attract hordes of opportunistic social climbers seeking their wealth.

c25:p0.text:
The minion of fortune and the worm of the hour, or in less cutting
      language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, the Golden Dustman, had become as
      much at home in his eminently aristocratic family mansion as he was likely
      ever to be. He could not but feel that, like an eminently aristocratic
      family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite
      amount of parasites; but he was content to regard this drawback on his
      property as a sort of perpetual Legacy Duty. He felt the more resigned to
      it, forasmuch as Mrs Boffin enjoyed herself completely, and Miss Bella was
      delighted.
c25:p0.summary: Nicodemus Boffin, the newly wealthy Golden Dustman, has settled into his grand mansion, finding it oversized but content because Mrs Boffin and Bella are delighted.
c25:p0.best_quote: like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c41:p1.text:
Yes, verily, my lords and gentlemen and honourable boards, adapting your
      Catechism to the occasion, and by God’s help so you must. For when we have
      got things to the pass that with an enormous treasure at disposal to
      relieve the poor, the best of the poor detest our mercies, hide their
      heads from us, and shame us by starving to death in the midst of us, it is
      a pass impossible of prosperity, impossible of continuance. It may not be
      so written in the Gospel according to Podsnappery; you may not ‘find these
      words’ for the text of a sermon, in the Returns of the Board of Trade; but
      they have been the truth since the foundations of the universe were laid,
      and they will be the truth until the foundations of the universe are
      shaken by the Builder. This boastful handiwork of ours, which fails in its
      terrors for the professional pauper, the sturdy breaker of windows and the
      rampant tearer of clothes, strikes with a cruel and a wicked stab at the
      stricken sufferer, and is a horror to the deserving and unfortunate. We
      must mend it, lords and gentlemen and honourable boards, or in its own
      evil hour it will mar every one of us.
c41:p1.summary: Dickens escalates his critique, invoking scripture to condemn a system where massive resources fail to relieve poverty, where the poor themselves reject institutional charity, creating a moral catastrophe that must be corrected or society will collapse.
c41:p1.best_quote: when we have got things to the pass that with an enormous treasure at disposal to relieve the poor, the best of the poor detest our mercies, hide their heads from us, and shame us by starving to death in the midst of us, it is a pass impossible of prosperity, impossible of continuance

c38:p0.text:
Were Bella Wilfer’s bright and ready little wits at fault, or was the
      Golden Dustman passing through the furnace of proof and coming out dross?
      Ill news travels fast. We shall know full soon.
c38:p0.summary: The opening poses the question of whether Bella's perception is faulty or whether Mr Boffin is being morally tested and corrupted by wealth.
c38:p0.best_quote: Was the Golden Dustman passing through the furnace of proof and coming out dross?

c63:p0.text:
In all the first bewilderment of her wonder, the most bewilderingly
      wonderful thing to Bella was the shining countenance of Mr Boffin. That
      his wife should be joyous, open-hearted, and genial, or that her face
      should express every quality that was large and trusting, and no quality
      that was little or mean, was accordant with Bella’s experience. But, that
      he, with a perfectly beneficent air and a plump rosy face, should be
      standing there, looking at her and John, like some jovial good spirit, was
      marvellous. For, how had he looked when she last saw him in that very room
      (it was the room in which she had given him that piece of her mind at
      parting), and what had become of all those crooked lines of suspicion,
      avarice, and distrust, that twisted his visage then?
c63:p0.summary: Bella marvels at Mr Boffin's completely transformed appearance and demeanor, wondering what happened to the suspicious, avaricious man she had last encountered in his home.
c63:p0.best_quote: what had become of all those crooked lines of suspicion, avarice, and distrust, that twisted his visage then?

c55:p58.text:
‘Not half, not a quarter, so much worthier as I hope you may some day find
      me! Try me through some reverse, John—try me through some trial—and
      tell them after  that , what you think of me.’
c55:p58.summary: Bella asks John to test her through adversity, wanting to prove she has genuinely transformed and is not merely a superficial convert to happiness.

c49:p72.text:
‘Upon which,’ pursued the cherub, ‘the certain mercenary young person
      distantly related to myself, having previously observed and mentioned to
      myself that prosperity was spoiling Mr Boffin, felt that she must not sell
      her sense of what was right and what was wrong, and what was true and what
      was false, and what was just and what was unjust, for any price that could
      be paid to her by any one alive? Am I leading up to it right?’

c63:p71.text:
‘O yes!’ cried Bella, covering her face with her hands; ‘but that I never
      shall be able to understand as long as I live. It is, how John could love
      me so when I so little deserved it, and how you, Mr and Mrs Boffin, could
      be so forgetful of yourselves, and take such pains and trouble, to make me
      a little better, and after all to help him to so unworthy a wife. But I am
      very very grateful.’
c63:p71.summary: Bella confesses her inability to comprehend how John could love her despite her unworthiness, and how the Boffins could invest such effort in her improvement and reformation.
c63:p71.best_quote: It is, how John could love me so when I so little deserved it, and how you, Mr and Mrs Boffin, could be so forgetful of yourselves, and take such pains and trouble, to make me a little better, and after all to help him to so unworthy a wife.

c23:p17.text:
‘Do me the favour,’ said Eugene, getting out of his chair with much
      gravity, ‘to come and inspect that feature of our establishment which you
      rashly disparage.’ With that, taking up a candle, he conducted his chum
      into the fourth room of the set of chambers—a little narrow room—which
      was very completely and neatly fitted as a kitchen. ‘See!’ said Eugene,
      ‘miniature flour-barrel, rolling-pin, spice-box, shelf of brown jars,
      chopping-board, coffee-mill, dresser elegantly furnished with crockery,
      saucepans and pans, roasting jack, a charming kettle, an armoury of
      dish-covers. The moral influence of these objects, in forming the domestic
      virtues, may have an immense influence upon me; not upon you, for you are
      a hopeless case, but upon me. In fact, I have an idea that I feel the
      domestic virtues already forming. Do me the favour to step into my
      bedroom. Secretaire, you see, and abstruse set of solid mahogany
      pigeon-holes, one for every letter of the alphabet. To what use do I
      devote them? I receive a bill—say from Jones. I docket it neatly at
      the secretaire,  Jones , and I put it into pigeonhole J. It’s the next thing
      to a receipt and is quite as satisfactory to  me . And I very much wish,
      Mortimer,’ sitting on his bed, with the air of a philosopher lecturing a
      disciple, ‘that my example might induce  you  to cultivate habits of
      punctuality and method; and, by means of the moral influences with which I
      have surrounded you, to encourage the formation of the domestic virtues.’
c23:p17.summary: Eugene conducts Mortimer through the chambers, cataloging the kitchen and bedroom with elaborate ironic commentary on how their furnishings cultivate domestic virtue while acknowledging his own hopelessness.
c23:p17.best_quote: The moral influence of these objects, in forming the domestic virtues, may have an immense influence upon me

c50:p75.text:
‘Don’t ask me. I desire to take no part in the discussion of these
      people’s affairs. I abhor the subject. It is an odious subject, an
      offensive subject, a subject that makes me sick, and I—’ And with
      his favourite right-arm flourish which sweeps away everything and settles
      it for ever, Mr Podsnap sweeps these inconveniently unexplainable wretches
      who have lived beyond their means and gone to total smash, off the face of
      the universe.
c50:p75.summary: Podsnap refuses to engage with the topic, declares it offensive and sickening, and uses his characteristic gesture to dismiss the entire matter.

c3:p118.text:
The Abbot replied with reticence, couldn’t say. If a murder, anybody might
      have done it. Burglary or pocket-picking wanted ’prenticeship. Not so,
      murder. We were all of us up to that. Had seen scores of people come to
      identify, and never saw one person struck in that particular way. Might,
      however, have been Stomach and not Mind. If so, rum stomach. But to be
      sure there were rum everythings. Pity there was not a word of truth in
      that superstition about bodies bleeding when touched by the hand of the
      right person; you never got a sign out of bodies. You got row enough out
      of such as her—she was good for all night now (referring here to the
      banging demands for the liver), ‘but you got nothing out of bodies if it
      was ever so.’
c3:p118.summary: The Inspector reflects reticently that if it is murder, anyone might have done it; murder requires no apprenticeship unlike burglary; he notes he has seen many people come to identify but never saw anyone react as Handford did; speculates whether it was stomach or mind; dismisses superstition about bodies bleeding when touched by guilty hands, noting you never get a sign from bodies.
c3:p118.best_quote: We were all of us up to that. Burglary or pocket-picking wanted 'prenticeship. Not so, murder.

c5:p154.text:
‘Commodious,’ gasped Mr Boffin, staring at the moon, after letting Wegg
      out at the gate and fastening it: ‘Commodious fights in that
      wild-beast-show, seven hundred and thirty-five times, in one character
      only! As if that wasn’t stunning enough, a hundred lions is turned into
      the same wild-beast-show all at once! As if that wasn’t stunning enough,
      Commodious, in another character, kills ’em all off in a hundred goes! As
      if that wasn’t stunning enough, Vittle-us (and well named too) eats six
      millions’ worth, English money, in seven months! Wegg takes it easy, but
      upon-my-soul to a old bird like myself these are scarers. And even now
      that Commodious is strangled, I don’t see a way to our bettering
      ourselves.’ Mr Boffin added as he turned his pensive steps towards the
      Bower and shook his head, ‘I didn’t think this morning there was half so
      many Scarers in Print. But I’m in for it now!’
c5:p154.summary: Outside the Bower, Boffin processes the shocking content of the reading: Commodus's 735 fights, Vittle-us's extravagant consumption, the hundred lions. He is both horrified and exhausted, realizing print contains many such 'scarers' but committed to continuing his education.
c5:p154.best_quote: 'Commodious fights in that wild-beast-show, seven hundred and thirty-five times, in one character only! As if that wasn't stunning enough...'

c66:p0.text:
Mr and Mrs John Harmon’s first delightful occupation was, to set all
      matters right that had strayed in any way wrong, or that might, could,
      would, or should, have strayed in any way wrong, while their name was in
      abeyance. In tracing out affairs for which John’s fictitious death was to
      be considered in any way responsible, they used a very broad and free
      construction; regarding, for instance, the dolls’ dressmaker as having a
      claim on their protection, because of her association with Mrs Eugene
      Wrayburn, and because of Mrs Eugene’s old association, in her turn, with
      the dark side of the story. It followed that the old man, Riah, as a good
      and serviceable friend to both, was not to be disclaimed. Nor even Mr
      Inspector, as having been trepanned into an industrious hunt on a false
      scent. It may be remarked, in connexion with that worthy officer, that a
      rumour shortly afterwards pervaded the Force, to the effect that he had
      confided to Miss Abbey Potterson, over a jug of mellow flip in the bar of
      the Six Jolly Fellowship Porters, that he ‘didn’t stand to lose a
      farthing’ through Mr Harmon’s coming to life, but was quite as well
      satisfied as if that gentleman had been barbarously murdered, and he (Mr
      Inspector) had pocketed the government reward.
c66:p0.summary: John and Mrs Harmon begin correcting wrongs caused by his supposed death, extending protection and aid to various characters including Riah and the dolls' dressmaker, while Inspector gossips about his satisfaction with Harmon's return.
c66:p0.best_quote: he 'didn't stand to lose a farthing' through Mr Harmon's coming to life, but was quite as well satisfied as if that gentleman had been barbarously murdered

c55:p146.text:

c3:p171.text:
Thus, like the tides on which it had been borne to the knowledge of men,
      the Harmon Murder—as it came to be popularly called—went up
      and down, and ebbed and flowed, now in the town, now in the country, now
      among palaces, now among hovels, now among lords and ladies and
      gentlefolks, now among labourers and hammerers and ballast-heavers, until
      at last, after a long interval of slack water it got out to sea and

c67:p60.text:
In my social experiences since Mrs Betty Higden came upon the scene and
      left it, I have found Circumlocutional champions disposed to be warm with
      me on the subject of my view of the Poor Law. My friend Mr Bounderby could
      never see any difference between leaving the Coketown ‘hands’ exactly as
      they were, and requiring them to be fed with turtle soup and venison out
      of gold spoons. Idiotic propositions of a parallel nature have been freely
      offered for my acceptance, and I have been called upon to admit that I
      would give Poor Law relief to anybody, anywhere, anyhow. Putting this
      nonsense aside, I have observed a suspicious tendency in the champions to
      divide into two parties; the one, contending that there are no deserving
      Poor who prefer death by slow starvation and bitter weather, to the
      mercies of some Relieving Officers and some Union Houses; the other,
      admitting that there are such Poor, but denying that they have any cause
      or reason for what they do. The records in our newspapers, the late
      exposure by  The Lancet , and the common sense and senses of common people,
      furnish too abundant evidence against both defences. But, that my view of
      the Poor Law may not be mistaken or misrepresented, I will state it. I
      believe there has been in England, since the days of the  Stuarts , no law
      so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law
      habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of
      disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the
      country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known
      language could say no more of their lawlessness.
c67:p60.summary: Dickens defends his critique of the Poor Law as grounded in observable fact and ethical principle, arguing it is the most infamously administered law in English history.

In the majority of the shameful cases of disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known language could say no more of their lawlessness.
